summary: Released canonical cover reference. Preserve the existing Green Corridor cover as the visual and trade-dress anchor for the Rex Fleet cover line; this recipe exists so the chef-facing cover shelf has a complete Issue 1–12 set, not to authorize redesign.
settingText: Released Rex Fleet Issue 1 cover composition from StarSplitterVisions: three-power frontier montage around Commodore Ella Venn and civilians, with Core/Fleet, Shard and Verge visual territories clearly separated.
panelPlan: REPRODUCTION / REFERENCE COVER. The released Issue 1 cover is already canon. Before any reproduction attempt, retrieve and pixel-read the exact canonical image at /images/covers/rex-fleet-issue-01-green-corridor.jpg from starsplitterrecords/StarSplitterVisions.

Match the released cover's portrait composition rather than reinterpreting it: enormous cream-and-gold REX FLEET masthead across the upper field; Star Splitter Visions mark top-left; ISSUE #1 block top-right; gold divider and tagline beneath the masthead; faction-emblem rhythm along the bottom.
Preserve the released image's central human hierarchy and three-way environmental split. Do not 'improve' the cast arrangement, faction geometry, palette, insignia, or typography.
This cover is the cover-brand anchor only. It is not an interior page-layout template and its montage composition is not mandatory for later issue covers.

directionInline.text: Released-canon lock: do not regenerate, redraw, modernize, relabel, or otherwise replace this cover unless the user explicitly reopens Issue 1 cover art. If a reproduction is specifically requested, the canonical cover pixels control the result.

title: Rex Fleet Issue 2 Cover
summary: Sell the rescue that costs Venn her command: a crippled mixed Verge–Shard evacuation ship is dying under fire while Thunderbreak visibly turns away from the authorized relief convoy to save the people nobody has permission to save.
settingText: Space outside Auric near a broken-moon passage; Thunderbreak bridge foreground framing a crippled civilian evacuation ship, distant authorized relief convoy, and incoming hostile fire.
panelPlan: ONE DOMINANT COVER IDEA: Venn is choosing the burning evacuation ship over the mission she was ordered to protect. Make that choice readable before any secondary detail.

Use a strong over-shoulder / three-quarter bridge composition: Venn in the lower foreground, controlled and unsentimental; beyond the bridge glass, the crippled evacuation vessel dominates the center. Thunderbreak's projected course bends toward it while the authorized relief convoy is visibly receding on the opposite vector.
The evacuation ship must look fragile, improvised and full of lives—not like a warship. Incoming attack geometry should create pressure without turning the cover into generic weapons spectacle.
Reserve the canonical upper masthead zone. The central civilian ship silhouette must remain readable beneath the title at thumbnail size.

Color logic: mature Fleet blue/gold/white around Venn and Thunderbreak; refugee vessel mixed/neutral civilian materials; restrained Shard red danger accents; green corridor/navigation state only where physically appropriate.
SPOILER CEILING: do not show Venn stripped of command, Abby turning on Billie, the hostage tug, the Crown Ring opening, or the final rescue outcome.

directionInline.text: Emotional promise: command under moral pressure. Venn is not posing heroically; she is making a costly operational decision. The cover should make the reader ask whether she can save the ship without losing everything else.

title: Rex Fleet Issue 3 Cover
summary: Sell Auric's impossible morning-after problem: the luxury ring has rooms, but 'empty' does not mean unowned, safe, warm, or politically available.
settingText: Auric Crown Ring luxury residence corridor during a heat failure; ornate doorway, abandoned personal belongings, emergency refugee bedding and failing environmental light.
panelPlan: ONE DOMINANT COVER IDEA: a beautiful apartment doorway has two legitimate claims on opposite sides. The architecture itself should divide the image.

Build the cover around one tall ornate open door beneath a failing chandelier. Inside: improvised refugee bedding, medicine, a child-sized blanket, cold breath and emergency light. Outside: preserved family possessions, framed personal objects and returning residents confronting the fact that the room was never truly abandoned.
Do not turn either side into villains. The tension comes from scarcity and incompatible need, not menace.

Use the doorway as the thumbnail silhouette and compositional spine. The luxury detailing should read immediately, but the cold emergency lighting must make it clear that luxury has become shelter rather than comfort.
Reserve the canonical masthead zone above the chandelier/door frame; keep the middle uncluttered enough that the doorway reads at phone-thumbnail scale.
SPOILER CEILING: do not show the sabotage culprit, Richard's evidence broadcast, Billie reaching the clinic, Tali's disappearance, the defense compact, or the ring's final survival state.

directionInline.text: Emotional promise: shelter turning into politics. The cover should make 'who gets this room?' feel as consequential as a fleet engagement.

title: Rex Fleet Issue 4 Cover
summary: Sell the Tal Corvus evacuation as a road that is simultaneously an escape route and a firing line: civilians have already started moving, and every armed faction knows exactly where they must pass.
settingText: Tal Corvus evacuation route through a narrow certified corridor volume; civilian transports and families moving toward safety while Fleet and Shard forces close around the route.
panelPlan: ONE DOMINANT COVER IDEA: a narrow green way out through a field of weapons. The civilians own the center of the composition; the armed powers squeeze the margins.

Use a deep vertical perspective down the evacuation corridor. A chain of civilian craft/boarding movement runs from bottom foreground toward a distant green beacon line. Fleet blue/gold ships and Shard red ships occupy opposing outer flanks, creating a literal corridor of threat without obscuring the people moving through it.
Place Tess near the lower route edge as the human focal point, facing the evacuation rather than the reader. She is holding the line, not striking a battle pose.
The green verified-route geometry must be physically legible and visually precious: one thin safe volume, not a giant portal tunnel.
Reserve the masthead zone in dark space. Thumbnail read should be 'thin green road, civilians in the middle, guns on both sides.'
SPOILER CEILING: do not depict the final coalition rescue, Pike/Billie outcomes, any specific ship defection, or the last families safely arriving.

directionInline.text: Emotional promise: evacuation under contested sovereignty. Spectacle is justified here, but the cover is about vulnerable movement through armed space, not who wins a battle.

title: Rex Fleet Issue 5 Cover
summary: Sell Jex Marrin's private route knowledge colliding with public hunger: the thing that made him powerful becomes impossible to keep private when people arrive needing a way through.
settingText: Jex Marrin's route room / Veil-adjacent broker space at the moment a hungry crowd reaches the threshold; layered route boards and a door opening onto waiting civilians.
panelPlan: ONE DOMINANT COVER IDEA: Jex stands between a private map and a public need. The threshold is the cover.

Frame Jex three-quarter at the doorway, older white-haired, short-bearded broker rather than action hero. Behind him, his dense route board glows with a few green safe lines and many dark/private branches. In front of him, the waiting crowd is compressed into silhouettes, food containers and exhausted faces rather than a threatening mob.
His hand should be near the route controls/markers, making the question visual: close the door or open the map.
The route board is valuable because it is specific and operational, not mystical. No floating hologram clutter and no generic cyberpunk data storm.
Reserve the masthead zone in darker ceiling/wall space. At thumbnail scale the reader should see one man, one doorway, one luminous route map, and people waiting outside.
SPOILER CEILING: do not show Jex giving all routes away, the later public distribution method, or any downstream attack caused by the route information.

directionInline.text: Emotional promise: information becoming a moral resource. The cover should make Jex's habitual instinct to sell knowledge collide visibly with the fact that the people at his door cannot afford the price.

title: Rex Fleet Issue 6 Cover
summary: Sell the instant Abby Saville's allegiance becomes a decision rather than a label: the Triarch has ordered civilian traffic stopped, the next crossing is open, and Abby is expected to enforce it.
settingText: Shard command bridge overlooking Auric Gate as a civilian convoy approaches a verified green crossing under armed Shard observation.
panelPlan: ONE DOMINANT COVER IDEA: Abby has a clean firing solution and civilians in the lane. The whole issue is contained in whether her hand completes the order.

Use a close-medium bridge composition with Abby in profile/three-quarter foreground, weapon-control light or command surface under one hand. Through the canopy/viewfield behind her, small civilian ships enter the green crossing while red Shard weapon vectors frame them.
Do not depict Abby as wavering helplessly. She is dangerous, composed and actively evaluating what obedience would mean.
The convoy should remain visibly civilian and small. The green safe-route state must contrast against the red Shard visual grammar without implying red is a beacon-safe state.
Keep the upper field simple for the canonical masthead. Thumbnail read: Abby + one hand at the control + green civilian line under red threat.
SPOILER CEILING: do not show Abby's refusal, captains siding with her, the crossing succeeding, or the Triarch losing control.

directionInline.text: Emotional promise: disobedience before it happens. The cover should make the reader feel the weight of an order that can still be obeyed.

title: Rex Fleet Issue 7 Cover
summary: Sell the Calm Corridor's impossible physics before anyone understands the solution: a perfectly ordered convoy sees an equally perfect duplicate where no second convoy can exist.
settingText: Inside the apparently calm corridor: clean low-tension geometry, ordered convoy formation, impossible duplicate convoy offset in physically wrong space, stars beginning to misregister.
panelPlan: ONE DOMINANT COVER IDEA: the convoy is looking at itself.

Use the central vertical axis as a false mirror plane without depicting literal glass. One convoy formation advances through clean corridor geometry; an identical formation appears displaced above/behind or across an impossible geometric fold, matching hulls and orientation too precisely to be another fleet.

The image should initially read as elegant symmetry, then become wrong on second glance: star fields do not align, distances contradict themselves, and the duplicate occupies space that should be empty.
Keep the physics restrained and measurable. No psychedelic kaleidoscope, portal vortex, ghost transparency, magical doubles or cosmic face imagery.
Use dark Warp Black depth with Fleet blue/gold/white and physically motivated green verified-route beacons; subtle violet/ion-white anomaly refraction may signal broken geometry.
Leave a clean masthead zone. Thumbnail read must be 'two identical convoys where only one should exist.'
SPOILER CEILING: do not reveal that breaking formation helps, do not show manual-control escape vectors, and do not depict the convoy already clear of the anomaly.

directionInline.text: Emotional promise: hard-SF uncertainty. The image should make an experienced navigator distrust sight without turning the phenomenon supernatural.

title: Rex Fleet Issue 8 Cover
summary: Sell the Shard challenge as politics compressed into a ritual circle: Tess Banks and Oren Pike face one another before the watching network, with command legitimacy reduced to the length of a blade.
settingText: Shard challenge circle / arena under hard practical light; ring of captains and observers, Tessa Banks and Oren Pike facing each other before the first decisive exchange.
panelPlan: ONE DOMINANT COVER IDEA: two people in a circle, one political order waiting on what happens between them.

Use a low, slightly wide arena composition. Tess and Pike stand separated across the circle with blades visible but not yet in contact. The surrounding captains form a dark ring that makes the empty space between them feel dangerous.
Tess must read as controlled and reluctant to become Pike's spectacle; Pike should read as someone who wants the spectacle. Neither should look like a fantasy gladiator.
Shard red can dominate the arena accents, but distinguish clothing, metal and practical shipboard/industrial construction from theatrical ritual fantasy.
Reserve upper darkness/structure for masthead. Thumbnail read: two distinct silhouettes, circular boundary, two blades, watching ring.
SPOILER CEILING: do not show Tess winning, Pike down, Tess refusing the kill, or captains changing sides.

directionInline.text: Emotional promise: legitimacy, violence and restraint. Sell the danger of the challenge without implying the issue's moral answer is simply 'who is better with a knife.'

title: Rex Fleet Issue 9 Cover
summary: Sell Jex Marrin becoming the target of the very network that made him valuable: Veil Market is hungry, route knowledge and money have converged around him, and too many people now know he knows where the food went.
settingText: Veil Market at night, dense but grounded working market lanes around Jex Marrin's position; route markers, closed stalls, ration scarcity and multiple lines of attention converging on him.
panelPlan: ONE DOMINANT COVER IDEA: every line in the market points at Jex.

Center Jex in a crowded Veil Market passage, not posing—moving or turning because he realizes the space around him has changed. Use awnings, catwalks, route lights and sightlines to converge subtly toward him.
Show scarcity through closed food shutters, empty containers and tense ordinary commerce. Show his value through a compact route slate/ledger or route-marking tool, not piles of money.

Allow one or two ambiguous distant figures to hold attention on him, but do not reveal an attacker, weapon, or attack method. The whole market should feel like a place Jex knows intimately that has suddenly become less safe.
Use deep market shadow with practical greens, dirty industrial light and restrained red accents; avoid neon cyberpunk cliché.
Reserve clear upper space for masthead. Thumbnail read: Jex isolated inside converging market geometry.
SPOILER CEILING: do not show the attempt on Jex's life, its failure, who paid for anything, his evidence release, or the Shatterforge connection.

directionInline.text: Emotional promise: conspiracy pressure at human scale. The reader should feel that Jex's knowledge has crossed the line from leverage to liability.

title: Rex Fleet Issue 10 Cover
summary: Sell Shatterforge as an engineered disaster masquerading as industrial failure: the Spire is overheating, workers are trapped, and the vents that should save them are visibly sealed.
settingText: Shatterforge industrial spire under runaway heat load; sealed vent structures glowing, workers trapped behind industrial geometry, approach path for Abby and Tess.
panelPlan: ONE DOMINANT COVER IDEA: a machine designed to vent heat is visibly cooking because its escape paths are shut.

Let Shatterforge dominate at monumental scale. Vertical industrial stacks and vent petals/panels are clamped or locked closed while internal orange-white heat blooms through seams. Workers appear as tiny human silhouettes behind gantries or windows to preserve the human stake.
Abby should be a small but clear figure advancing into the structure on a lower gantry/approach; Tess is behind or arriving after her, making pursuit/rescue legible without revealing outcomes.

The cover may show that the vents are mechanically locked because the next-issue teaser already establishes that fact. It must not reveal who ordered it, where the proof is found, or what happens to Abby.
Use industrial yellow/white heat against dark structure, with Shard red accents and Fleet/Verge colors only where story-appropriate. Do not make the Spire a fantasy volcano.
Reserve upper smoke/dark-space geometry for masthead. Thumbnail read: gigantic sealed industrial structure glowing from within, two tiny people going toward it.
SPOILER CEILING: do not show the evidence package, Abby's disappearance, any final escape, or the identity/motive behind the sabotage.

directionInline.text: Emotional promise: industrial rescue plus conspiracy. Spectacle comes from physical systems failing on purpose, not from arbitrary explosions.

title: Rex Fleet Issue 11 Cover
summary: Sell Auric Gate at the edge of renewed war just as impossible Rift duplicates make targeting itself untrustworthy: everybody has a target until nobody can be sure what they are aiming at.
settingText: Auric Gate standoff in open space: Fleet and Shard formations facing one another, weapon locks active, a physically impossible duplicate ship appearing between or overlapping the lines, stressed corridor geometry.
panelPlan: ONE DOMINANT COVER IDEA: two armed lines are ready to fire and a ship that should not exist has appeared exactly where certainty is required.

Use opposing diagonals: Fleet blue/gold ships from one side, Shard red ships from the other, weapons visually trained across a narrow central void. In that void, place one impossible duplicate ship/echo with geometry that contradicts the known formation.
The duplicate must look materially real enough to be targetable, not translucent or ghostly. Its wrongness should come from identity/position: same hull where no second hull can be.
Avoid showing an actual broadside or explosion. This is the fraction of a second before disaster, when targeting lights are on and restraint still exists as a possible action.
Rift anomaly treatment stays physical and restrained: Warp Black depth, ion-white/violet geometric stress, no mystical portal.
Reserve masthead space in the upper dark field. Thumbnail read: two opposing fleets, one impossible ship in the crossfire.
SPOILER CEILING: do not show weapons being lowered, the Mirror Star collapsing, Billie stopping Pike, or the battle's final de-escalation.

directionInline.text: Emotional promise: brinkmanship under epistemic failure. The cover should make 'hold your fire' feel like the most dangerous command in the book without printing that phrase.

title: Rex Fleet Issue 12 Cover
summary: Sell the first Shattered Accord as the harder work after the guns stop: people who were shooting at one another yesterday have to write rules today because another convoy is already coming.
settingText: Functional negotiation room overlooking Auric Gate; unsigned agreement centered on a table, Fleet/Verge/Shard representatives around it, next civilian convoy visible approaching the green crossing beyond the window.
panelPlan: ONE DOMINANT COVER IDEA: the next convoy is coming whether the people at the table agree or not.

Compose from slightly above table height so an unsigned document occupies the visual center, surrounded by distinct hands, sleeves and restrained faction cues from Fleet, Verge and Shard participants. Faces may be present around the upper/middle composition, but nobody should dominate like a victor.

Through a large window behind them, Auric Gate and a small incoming civilian convoy are visible approaching the verified green route. The outside movement creates the deadline; the paper creates the conflict.

Keep weapons absent from hands but not erased from the world—holsters, ship silhouettes or the scarred Gate can remind the reader what yesterday looked like without turning the cover back into a battle poster.
Do not show signatures, a completed agreement, celebratory unity, handshakes, or a resolved political hierarchy. The document must remain visibly unsigned/unsettled.
Use Fleet blue/gold/white, Verge/public-route green, and restrained Shard red as separate accents rather than blending them into a new unity palette.
Reserve canonical masthead space above the window. Thumbnail read: unsigned paper, incompatible hands around it, convoy coming in behind.
SPOILER CEILING: do not reveal the Accord's final terms, who signs, whether anyone gains command authority, or the final editorial return message.

directionInline.text: Emotional promise: governance as suspense. The cover should make writing rules before the next crossing feel as urgent as the firefight that preceded it.
